title: Neural Networks in Trading: A Spatio-Temporal State Space Model for Financial Data Analysis (STSSM Block)
text:
Introduction
The
E-STMFlow
framework is a rare example of an approach that promises efficiency and fits seamlessly into the logic of real financial markets. In
the previous article
, we explored the approaches proposed by the framework’s authors and got a sense of the architecture’s character — its emphasis on compactness, precision, and respect for the structure of the data being analyzed. And now, before continuing with the practical implementation, it is helpful to review the big picture once again. This helps not only to refresh your memory, but also to immerse yourself once again in the logic behind the authors' approach.
The authors have created an architecture that handles event streams very naturally. The data here is irregular and chaotic. This is very similar to how the market behaves. The price on the chart does not move in a straight line. Trading volume comes in bursts, and ticks arrive at varying rates. To extract meaning from such streams, events are first converted into a structured tensor — a three-dimensional grid that records the coordinates and time of each change. Think of it as a structured tick tape, where every movement and every pause matters. This is how the authors prepare the data stream so that the model can process it without losing any information.
The resulting tensor is passed to the
Spatio-Temporal Encoder
— the key module of the architecture. It transforms the stream of events into a set of features that form a picture of the motion. The
Encoder
detects local fluctuations and relates them to the overall dynamics. The model responds to the stream rhythm rather than to individual values. For tasks where the speed of response to changes is important, this approach offers a significant advantage.
At the heart of the encoder is the
Spatio-Temporal State Space Model
(
STSSM
). This module processes a volume of events in layers, preserving spatial patterns and taking into account their chronological sequence. As a result, the model perceives the stream as a whole: it understands impulses, pauses, and their combinations. In the context of financial markets, this is akin to the ability to detect the onset of a trend reversal or rising volatility before traditional indicators pick up on it.
STSSM
generates a robust representation of the data, enabling the model to distinguish between significant events and ordinary noise.
Subsequent levels of the architecture transform these features into a concrete result. In the authors' study, this result is a dense optical flow map, but the principle is universal. The model carefully prepares the signal without burdening the system with unnecessary computations. Even at the encoder level, it's clear why the solution works effectively. It is compact, cohesive, and does not complicate natural processes. In financial markets, this means being able to process a stream of ticks quickly and without delay, capturing every significant market impulse.
The authors emphasize resource efficiency. Their approach is faster than many traditional architectures, including transformers and convolutional models with a large number of layers. By properly handling the stream of events, the model obtains the maximum amount of information at minimal cost. The encoder acts as a filter, removing unnecessary data and generating signals that provide a real advantage in data stream processing.
Another important point is maintaining temporal consistency. The event stream may be erratic, with sudden spikes and long pauses. The encoder creates a sequential representation that reflects the internal stream rhythm without sacrificing local precision. In financial markets, this is equivalent to a trader recognizing that a sharp market impulse may be lurking behind a period of calm and reacting to it in a timely manner.
Importantly, the authors' approach remains simple in essence. Everything is based on precise event discretization,
STSSM
processing, and compact convolutions. This solution demonstrates that powerful analytics are possible without unnecessary complexity, and that is precisely what makes
E-STMFlow
appealing for practical applications.
The authors' visualization of the
E-STMFlow
framework is shown below.
In the previous
article
, we decided to apply the approaches proposed by the framework's authors to the field of spiking solutions. This is entirely consistent with the logic of event-driven models. Furthermore, we have implemented an embedding stack that neatly prepares the event stream, creating a convenient structure for further analysis. It acts as a filter, allowing the model to recognize rhythm and patterns.
Today we're taking the next step and beginning to implement the
heart
of the encoder — the
STSSM
block. It is this module that will link local events to the global dynamics of the stream, creating a stable representation of the data. This is particularly important for financial data streams. The market never moves in a straight line. Ticks arrive at varying rates, and volumes can change instantaneously. The
STSSM
block will allow the model to perceive these impulses holistically, treat pauses and bursts as part of the bigger picture, and extract key features for further analysis.
Moving on to the practical part of the work, it is important to emphasize right away that the
STSSM
block is not just a module, but a complex, multi-level structure comprising several interconnected components. Its architecture resembles a carefully designed machine in which each part plays its own role, and together they provide a holistic view of the event stream. To make the process clear and easy to follow, we will build the block step by step, working our way up through its hierarchy from the bottom. This approach helps you avoid getting lost in the details and ensures you have a clear understanding of how each element contributes to the final result.
Spike-SSM
Module
The first step will be to implement the
SSM
module. This component can be compared to the foundation of a building: it provides the basis for event processing, neatly organizing the stream and capturing its internal dynamics. In a financial context, this is similar to the work of a trader who first closely monitors changes in volume and price fluctuations before drawing conclusions about the market’s direction. The
SSM
module performs a similar function: it detects local changes and uses them to generate structured features that will be used at subsequent levels of the block.
We have repeatedly discussed the importance of taking into account both temporal and spatial dependencies when analyzing event streams. In this work, the
2D-SSM
module is used to implement this functionality; it is capable of detecting changes not only over time but also across various data dimensions. In a market analogy, this is similar to a trader who simultaneously monitors price fluctuations and trading volume, relating each movement to the overall market context. For the spiking version of the algorithm, we implement a new class,
CNeuronSpike2DSSMOCL
, which inherits the basic capabilities of the neural element and adapts them to work with streams of spiking events.

The class architecture is designed as a finely tuned system of filters and transformation stages.
Hidden states
capture the current dynamics of the stream, just as a trader keeps the latest market impulses in mind.
Projections along the temporal and spatial axes
allow us to relate local changes to the overall picture, as if we were comparing instantaneous price fluctuations with the overall trend for the day.
Convolution blocks
(
cA
,
cBC_Time
,
cBC_Variable
, and others) identify significant changes in the stream by filtering out noise, just as an experienced analyst separates random spikes in volume from a genuine market impulse.
The initialization method defines the internal architecture of the
2D-SSM
module and sets all the key parameters necessary for its stable operation. If we draw an analogy with trading, this process is similar to setting up a workspace. The observation windows and the number of
financial instruments
to analyze are determined, indicators are activated, and resources are prepared to process the stream of ticks. Without such preparation, any model loses its sensitivity to signals and risks missing important impulses.

false

The algorithm begins by passing control to the parent class, where resources are allocated for the threads and the overall structure is defined. The activation function is disabled to ensure that data is transmitted without distortion.
The
iWindowOut
and
iUnitsOut
parameters specify the size of the output window and the number of elements in the sequence — this is the foundation that determines how much information will be included in each time slice. For financial data streams, this is similar to choosing a time frame and the number of candlesticks to observe in order to capture both short-term and medium-term market impulses.
iWindowOut = window_out;
   iUnitsOut = units_out;
Next, projection blocks along the time axis (
cProjectionX_Time
) and the variable axis (
cProjectionX_Variable
) are created. For a temporal projection, the data passes through a chain consisting of a transposition, a convolution, and another transposition.

index =
0
;

NULL
;

NULL
;

new
CNeuronTransposeOCL();
if
(!transp ||

0
, index, OpenCL, units_in, window_in, optimization, iBatch) ||

return
false
;

new

if

0

, optimization, iBatch) ||

return

new

if

return

In practice, this is similar to analyzing a tick stream. First, we change the observation perspective; then, we evaluate local impulses and trends; and finally, we map the data back to the original space to integrate it with other data streams.
A projection along the variable axis links events to various aspects of the market — volume, the rate of price change, and the strength of market impulses. So the model perceives not just movement, but its structure.

cHiddenStates

A

2

It is worth noting that both components contain information for analyzing both temporal and spatial aspects. As a result, they can be processed simultaneously in parallel threads, which significantly speeds up data processing and allows the model to respond to market changes in near real time.
Block
BC
serves as the link between the module's core and matrices
B
and
C

index++;

B
and
C

Delta
blocks (
cDelta_Time
and *
cDelta_Variable

For example, a sharp spike in volume or a short-term price surge is immediately recorded and influences future forecasts, just as if an experienced trader were taking instantaneous volatility into account.

Each step of the initialization process is thoroughly checked. If an element cannot be created, the resources are released, preventing errors and crashes.
At the end, the
Clear
method is called, which clears all intermediate states and prepares the object to process the first data stream. In a financial market context, this is like
a warm-up
before a trading session — the model is ready to respond to any impulses without losing focus or structure.
As a result, the initialization method creates a complete
2D-SSM
module architecture, allowing the model to view the stream of events as a single, cohesive process.
The forward pass algorithm in
2D-SSM
is implemented in the
feedForward
method. It can be thought of as a virtual trading session. The tick stream passes through a series of analytical filters, each of which performs a specific task. First, the data enters the
Projection Time
chain, where each block processes events along the time axis. It is as if a trader were closely monitoring every candlestick on the chart: noting short-term fluctuations, market impulses, and sharp price movements. Each element of the projection carefully filters the signal, isolating the important parts and passing them on.
bool
CNeuronSpike2DSSMOCL::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL * NeuronOCL)
  {
   CNeuronBaseOCL *inp = NeuronOCL;
   CNeuronBaseOCL *x_time =
NULL
;
   CNeuronBaseOCL *x_var =
NULL
;
//--- Projection Time
int
total = cProjectionX_Time.Total();
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < total; i++)
     {
      x_time = cProjectionX_Time.At(i);
if
(!x_time ||
         !x_time.FeedForward(inp))
return
false
;
      inp = x_time;
     }
The data stream is then routed to
Projection Variable
, where other aspects of the market are analyzed: trading volume, the rate of price change, and the strength of market impulses. Here, the model
looks
at the market from a different perspective — the parameter space — by linking events together. Processing these two projections in parallel allows us to see both local spikes and the overall market dynamics at the same time.
//--- Projection Variable
inp = NeuronOCL;
   total = cProjectionX_Variable.Total();
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < total; i++)
     {
      x_var = cProjectionX_Variable.At(i);
if
(!x_var ||
         !x_var.FeedForward(inp))
return
false
;
      inp = x_var;
     }
The next stage involves the core of the model. Block
A
accumulates information about hidden states, forming the basis for forecasting.
if
(!cA.FeedForward(cHiddenStates.AsObject()))
return
false
;
The
BC
blocks simultaneously generate matrices
B
and
C
, which are then stored separately in dedicated buffers.
if
(!cBC_Time.FeedForward(x_time) ||
      !cBC_Variable.FeedForward(x_var))
return
false
;
if
(!DeConcat(cB_Time.getOutput(), cC_Time.getOutput(), cBC_Time.getOutput(),
1
, iUnitsOut, iUnitsOut) ||
      !DeConcat(cB_Variable.getOutput(), cC_Variable.getOutput(), cBC_Variable.getOutput(),
1
, iUnitsOut, iUnitsOut))
return
false
;
It is similar to the work of an experienced analyst who creates several charts at once, combines them, and identifies patterns so as not to miss a single important signal.
Delta
blocks track changes in state over time and across variables, adjusting the forecast accordingly.
if
(!cDelta_Time.FeedForward(x_time) ||
      !cDelta_Variable.FeedForward(x_var))
return
false
;
We also save the last hidden state, which we will need for the backward pass.
if
(!cHiddenStates.SwapOutputs())
return
false
;
//---
return
feedForwardSSM2D();
  }
Finally, the method calls
feedForwardSSM2D
, which carefully combines all signals into a single structured stream within the
OpenCL
context. As a result, the model receives a representation of the market that is ready for analysis. It simultaneously captures short-term market impulses, integrates them into the broader context, and develops a comprehensive understanding of price and volume dynamics. This approach makes it possible to forecast market movements with a high degree of accuracy, based on the actual structure of the event stream rather than on isolated data points.
Once the model has generated a prediction, the next step is
learning from errors
, which we implement in the
calcInputGradients
method. If we draw an analogy with trading, it is similar to the review of a closed position. We compare the forecast with actual market fluctuations and determine where the model fell short. This will allow us to make more accurate predictions next time.
bool
CNeuronSpike2DSSMOCL::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL * NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!NeuronOCL)
return
false
;
//---
if
(!calcInputGradientsSSM2D())
return
false
;
First, the method calls
calcInputGradientsSSM2D
, where the errors obtained at the object's output are distributed across the
2D-SSM
structure, capturing discrepancies both over time and across variables.
Next, the gradients of blocks
B
and
C
, formed by the
BC
module, are carefully combined into a single tensor.
if
(!Concat(cB_Time.getGradient(), cC_Time.getGradient(), cBC_Time.getGradient(),
1
, iUnitsOut, iUnitsOut) ||
      !Concat(cB_Variable.getGradient(), cC_Variable.getGradient(), cBC_Variable.getGradient(),
1
, iUnitsOut, iUnitsOut))
return
false
;
Deactivating the outputs of the intermediate blocks — time and variable projections,
BC
matrices, delta blocks, and block
A
— adjusts the resulting error gradients using the derivatives of the corresponding activation functions.
//--- Deactivation
CNeuronBaseOCL *x_time = cProjectionX_Time[-
1
];
   CNeuronBaseOCL *x_var = cProjectionX_Variable[-
1
];
if
(!x_time || !x_var)
return
false
;
   Deactivation(x_time)
   Deactivation(x_var)
   Deactivation(cBC_Time)
   Deactivation(cBC_Variable)
   Deactivation(cDelta_Time)
   Deactivation(cDelta_Variable)
   Deactivation(cA)
Next, we need to propagate gradients back to the temporal and spatial projections. However, these projections already contain part of the error gradient from the SSM operations, so the subsequent operations must preserve the existing data. First, let's transfer the error gradients from the
BC
modules and add them to the previously obtained values.
//--- Gradients to X projections
CBufferFloat *grad_x_time = x_time.getGradient();
   CBufferFloat *grad_x_var = x_var.getGradient();
if
(!x_time.SetGradient(x_time.getPrevOutput(),
false
) ||
      !x_var.SetGradient(x_var.getPrevOutput(),
false
))
return
false
;
//--- BC -> X
if
(!x_time.CalcHiddenGradients(cBC_Time.AsObject()) ||
      !SumAndNormilize(grad_x_time, x_time.getGradient(), grad_x_time, iWindowOut,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
if
(!x_var.CalcHiddenGradients(cBC_Variable.AsObject()) ||
      !SumAndNormilize(grad_x_var, x_var.getGradient(), grad_x_var, iWindowOut,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
Next, we pass the gradients from the
Delta
blocks.
//--- Delta -> X
if
(!x_time.CalcHiddenGradients(cDelta_Time.AsObject()) ||
      !SumAndNormilize(grad_x_time, x_time.getGradient(), grad_x_time, iWindowOut,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
if
(!x_var.CalcHiddenGradients(cDelta_Variable.AsObject()) ||
      !SumAndNormilize(grad_x_var, x_var.getGradient(), grad_x_var, iWindowOut,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
if
(!x_time.SetGradient(grad_x_time,
false
) ||
      !x_var.SetGradient(grad_x_var,
false
))
return
false
;
The gradients are then propagated along the
Projection Variable
and
Projection Time
chains from the end to the beginning. Every deviation — whether it is a sharp spike in volume, a momentum candle, or a brief pause in price movement — is carefully taken into account and integrated into the overall market picture.
//--- Projection Variable
int
total = cProjectionX_Variable.Total() -
2
;
for
(
int
i = total; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
      x_var = cProjectionX_Variable[i];
if
(!x_var ||
         !x_var.CalcHiddenGradients(cProjectionX_Variable[i +
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
//--- Projection Time
total = cProjectionX_Time.Total() -
2
;
for
(
int
i = total; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
      x_time = cProjectionX_Time[i];
if
(!x_time ||
         !x_time.CalcHiddenGradients(cProjectionX_Time[i +
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
Finally, the adjusted gradients are propagated back to the model's input, allowing the neuron weights to be updated and the system to be prepared for the next training iteration.
//--- Projections -> inputs
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(x_var.AsObject()))
return
false
;
   grad_x_time = NeuronOCL.getGradient();
if
(!NeuronOCL.SetGradient(x_time.getPrevOutput(),
false
) ||
      !NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(x_time.AsObject()) ||
      !SumAndNormilize(grad_x_time, NeuronOCL.getGradient(), grad_x_time,
1
,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
) ||
      !NeuronOCL.SetGradient(grad_x_time,
false
))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
Thus,
calcInputGradients

Conclusion
The
STSSM
block we have optimized and its derivatives do not merely replicate the ideas of the framework's authors; they develop them further with a practical focus on real-world market challenges. During the implementation process, we did not limit ourselves to strictly following the original architecture. Key components were optimized for
MQL5
and
OpenCL
, enabling high computational density and stable performance even with large time windows and a wide range of variables.
The main advantage of the
STSSM
approach is its ability to analyze temporal and spatial dynamics simultaneously. Our implementation makes this process particularly efficient through parallel computational threads, an improved normalization system, and a carefully designed projection-layer structure.
Thus, the resulting architecture combines the theoretical strength of the original framework with the practical applicability of our optimizations. We now have a flexible, scalable, and resource-efficient tool ready for testing under challenging financial market conditions.
